title: The Orphan of Zhao
subtitle: Loyalty and Righteousness Shake Heaven and Earth; Hot Blood Illuminates a Thousand Autumns
description: "The Orphan of Zhao," full title "Revenge of the Orphan of Zhao," is a Yuan-dynasty play by Ji Junxiang, based on the "Biography of the Zhao Clan" in the "Records of the Grand Historian." It tells the story of the Spring and Autumn period, when Tu'an Gu of the State of Jin massacred the entire Zhao clan, and Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu sacrificed their own sons and lives to save the orphan Zhao Wu, who took his revenge fifteen years later. This was the first Chinese drama translated into Europe; Voltaire's adaptation, "The Orphan of China," caused a sensation in eighteenth-century Paris.

route.title: The Orphan of Zhao: The Road of Loyalty and Righteousness Through a Thousand Autumns
route.intro:
Propping up my sickly body, I endure; I will plunge straight into the tiger's lair. All that matters is that the orphan finds his fortune.
Ji Junxiang, a native of Dadu (present-day Beijing) in the Yuan dynasty, vanished into historical obscurity—yet with one play, "The Orphan of Zhao," he captured the most soul-shaking spirit of loyalty and righteousness in Chinese culture. The story first appeared in the "Zuo Zhuan" and the "Records of the Grand Historian," was brought to the stage in the Yuan dynasty, and in the eighteenth century, through Voltaire, spread to the world—a path of loyalty and duty stretching from the blood-drenched Spring and Autumn period of the State of Jin to the Enlightenment of Paris. Let us enter the depths of Mount Zang in Yu County, Shanxi, and in the millenary ancient shrine that once hid the Orphan of Zhao, feel that timeless loyalty and great righteousness.

stops.title: Stop One: Tu'an Gu Massacres the Zhao Clan
stops.content: In the late Spring and Autumn period, one of the most powerful ministerial clans in the State of Jin—the Zhao clan—held sway over the court and government. Tu'an Gu, the favored minister of Duke Ling of Jin, deeply resented Zhao's power and meticulously laid a deadly trap. He first had a ferocious dog trained to attack anyone wearing the clothes of Zhao Dun. Then he falsely accused Zhao Dun of treason, claiming the dog was proof of his treachery—"the divine hound discerns the villain." The dim-witted Duke Ling accepted this accusation, and Tu'an Gu led troops to massacre the entire Zhao clan, over three hundred people. Only one person escaped—Zhuang Ji, Zhao Shuo's wife and the elder sister of Duke Cheng of Jin, who was pregnant and hiding in the palace. She gave birth to a baby boy. This was the sole surviving bloodline of the Zhao clan—Zhao Wu. When the news reached Tu'an Gu, he immediately ordered the palace sealed and the infant searched for: "To pull the weeds, you must dig up the roots; do not let the sprout grow." An epic battle to find and save the orphan had begun. On this land drenched in blood and fire, the political center of the State of Jin at that time lay in present-day Houma and Quwo—the Houma Jin State Ruins, the site of Jin's final capital "Xintian." The "Houma Covenant Texts" unearthed here are the earliest surviving brush-written manuscripts in China—those covenant oaths written in cinnabar on jade tablets record the life-and-death alliances and bloody power struggles among the Jin ministerial clans in that age of the Zhao orphan.

stops.title: Stop Two: Cheng Ying Sacrifices His Son to Save the Orphan
stops.content: Among the retainers of the Zhao clan was a man named Cheng Ying. He was not a blood relative, not even an important retainer—just an ordinary hanger-on who kept accounts and ran errands. Yet after the Zhao clan was wiped out, he made a decision no one could understand: to exchange his own son for the life of the Zhao orphan. The plan was even crueler than the story. Cheng Ying himself went to Tu'an Gu to report that the orphan was hidden in the home of the old retainer Gongsun Chujiu. Tu'an Gu led troops to search; Gongsun Chujiu feigned panic and denial, but eventually they found a swaddled infant—Cheng Ying's own son. Tu'an Gu sneered, drew his sword, and in front of Cheng Ying, dashed the baby onto the stone steps, killing him. Gongsun Chujiu, eyes blazing with fury, cursed Tu'an Gu for his brutality and was run through with a sword. The blood splattered onto the yellow earth, quickly turning brown under the scorching sun. Through it all, Cheng Ying's expression did not change. He even bowed to Tu'an Gu and said, "Thank you, General"—watching his own flesh and blood become a bloody mess on the stone steps, watching his longtime friend fall in a pool of blood, all to protect the real orphan Zhao Wu, hidden right under Tu'an Gu's nose. This is the most brutal and most heroic "bait-and-switch" in Chinese literary history. In the play, Ji Junxiang has Cheng Ying sing his heart-rending pain: "I exchange this son of my own for that orphan of another." Just one line, no rhetoric, no elaboration—because any rhetoric is pale before such sacrifice. Why did Cheng Ying exchange his own son's life for another man's son's life? He sought no fame—he bore the infamy of "betraying friends for personal gain" for fifteen years, the whole world cursing him as a base, unscrupulous villain. He sought no profit—after the orphan took his revenge, the first thing Cheng Ying did was go to Gongsun Chujiu's grave and fall on his own sword. There is only one explanation: righteousness. Not loyalty to a master, but loyalty to the Way. In Cheng Ying's world, there was something more precious than life, closer than blood, worth protecting beyond all worldly honor and disgrace—and that was "yi"—righteousness. This story unfolded on the land of the State of Jin. From the Houma Jin State Ruins, the remains of the final Jin capital "Xintian," unearthed the "Houma Covenant Texts"—oath words written in cinnabar on jade tablets, those blood-red characters recording the life-and-death struggles among Jin's ministerial clans in the age of the Zhao orphan. Each jade tablet is like a contract soaked in blood, bearing witness to an age where loyalty and treachery were indistinguishable, where life and death hung by a thread. Further north to Taiyuan, the Jin Shrine's Holy Mother Hall stands majestically—this millenary shrine commemorating the founding ruler of Jin, Tang Shuyu, is the starting point for understanding this history. Inside, the Song-dynasty painted clay statues of maidservants—some holding seals, some presenting kerchiefs, some standing with bowed heads—their expressions unchanged by a thousand years. Those silently serving countenances—are they not the embodiment of nameless loyalists like Gongsun Chujiu and Cheng Ying? The ancient buildings of the Three Jin lands are scattered like stars, but what touches the heart most are those spirits of loyalty and righteousness echoing through the mountains and rivers, that will never decay.

stops.title: Stop Three: Hiding the Orphan on Mount Zang for Fifteen Years
stops.content: The real orphan Zhao Wu was secretly taken out of the palace by Cheng Ying and hidden deep in the mountains of Yu County—which thereafter was named Mount Zang (Hiding Mountain). In a hidden cave on the mountain, Cheng Ying raised the orphan, passing himself off as a woodcutter. Fifteen years, over five thousand days and nights, every moment filled with fear; fifteen years, from a crying infant to a vigorous youth. The shrine that bears witness to this legendary act of loyalty—the Mount Zang Shrine—still stands deep in Mount Zang, Yu County, Shanxi. The Ming-dynasty building complex is built into the mountainside, halls and pavilions layered one above another—the mountain gate, main hall, and Orphan-Hiding Cave arranged in succession. Stepping into the Orphan-Hiding Cave, you can almost feel Cheng Ying's body heat as he huddled in the darkness with the infant. That nameless retainer traded fifteen years of solitude for the continuation of a bloodline, forging the hardest backbone of Chinese culture.

stops.title: Stop Four: The Orphan Takes Revenge, Great Righteousness Shines Forth
stops.content: Fifteen years passed. After Duke Dao of Jin ascended the throne, the truth came to light, and the identity of the Orphan of Zhao was revealed to the world. The infant of years past had grown into the valiant young man Zhao Wu. Cheng Ying told him, one by one, the truth of the Zhao clan's annihilation. Zhao Wu wept and swore revenge. In the end, Tu'an Gu was executed, the Zhao clan's fief was restored, and Zhao Wu revived the family. As for Cheng Ying—the man who had sacrificed his own son's life for the Zhao family, who had borne fifteen years of infamy—he went calmly to Gongsun Chujiu's grave and took his own life. He said: "In the disaster of the lower palace, all could have died. I did not die because I wished to establish the Zhao heir. Now that the Zhao heir has been established, has become an adult, and has been restored to his former rank, I shall go below to report to Zhao Xuanmeng and Gongsun Chujiu." He had lived for fifteen years only to fulfill one promise. The story of the Orphan of Zhao took place in the State of Jin, and the roots of Jin are in Taiyuan. The Jin Shrine commemorates the founding ruler of Jin, Tang Shuyu. Its Song-dynasty painted clay maidservant statues are hailed as one of the "Three Wonders of the Jin Shrine"; the Never-Aging Spring flows ceaselessly. Standing before the Holy Mother Hall, gazing at those silent statues that have endured for a thousand years, you think of Cheng Ying, Gongsun Chujiu—those remembered and forgotten by history. The most precious thing on the land of the Three Jins is not the ancient buildings, but the spirits of loyalty and righteousness that echo through the mountains and rivers.

stops.title: Stop Five: From Mount Zang to Paris
stops.content: In the eighteenth century, the French Jesuit missionary Joseph de Prémare translated "The Orphan of Zhao" into French. When Voltaire read the play, he was profoundly moved—an ancient Eastern nation possessed such sublime moral spirit! He adapted it, creating "L'Orphelin de la Chine" ("The Orphan of China"), relocating the story to the Song-Yuan transition and transforming Cheng Ying into a scholar, elevating the theme to "civilization conquering barbarism." In 1755, "L'Orphelin de la Chine" premiered in Paris, causing a citywide sensation. For the first time, the thinkers of the Enlightenment saw in Eastern drama the values of reason and moral power that they cherished. Voltaire said: "This play vividly and clearly demonstrates the greatness of the Chinese spirit—that is, loyalty, justice, and self-sacrifice." From a mountain cave in the Spring and Autumn period of the State of Jin to the brilliantly lit opera houses of eighteenth-century Paris—a story of loyalty and sacrifice traveled two thousand years and halfway across the globe. The Orphan-Hiding Cave of the Mount Zang Shrine contains no gold or silver treasure, but what it holds is the most precious thing in all humanity. It tells everyone who enters: in this world, some things are more valuable than life. If you have the opportunity, start from the Jin Shrine in Taiyuan, pass through the Houma Jin State Ruins to trace the remains of the Jin capital, and finally come to Mount Zang in Yu County. Stand before the Orphan-Hiding Cave—you will hear the wind of 2,600 years ago blowing through the mountains. In that wind is a father's call to his son, and an honorable man's final reckoning with his promise.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Millenary Wooden Pagoda Bears Witness to Loyalty
stops.content:
Leaving Mount Zang in Yu County and heading north, through Yanmen Pass and across the Sanggan River, you arrive at Ying County. Here stands a monument even older and taller than the Mount Zang Shrine—the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda, also known as the Sakyamuni Pagoda of Fogong Temple. Built in the second year of the Qingning reign of the Liao dynasty (1056), it rises sixty-seven meters high. The entire pagoda is assembled from hundreds of thousands of wooden components fitted together with mortise and tenon joints, without a single nail or piece of iron. It is the oldest and tallest extant wooden pagoda in the world.

For 960 years, the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda has weathered dozens of earthquakes and countless wars. Even in 1926, during the conflicts between warlords, it was struck by artillery shells—yet it still stands unshakable, like an unyielding backbone rising from the land of the Three Jins. Climbing the pagoda and looking in all directions, the Northern Sacred Mountain Hengshan looms like a screen, the Sanggan River winds like a ribbon. The northern wind passes through the layered brackets of the eaves; the copper bells at the corners chime—like loyal spirits from a thousand years ago whispering softly.

In the age when Cheng Ying hid the orphan on Mount Zang, this pagoda had not yet been built. Two thousand years later, when the Liao people stacked layer upon layer of wooden beams to build it skyward, the story of the Orphan of Zhao had already spread throughout the Central Plains. The Wooden Pagoda and the Mount Zang Shrine—one in the east, one in the west—echo each other across the distance. One, with its ingenious mortise-and-tenon joints, has supported 960 years of wind and frost; the other, with its self-sacrificing spirit of loyalty, has pierced through 2,600 years of time. Standing beneath this millenary pagoda and looking up, the eaves soar toward the sky. You suddenly understand: there are things in this world harder than steel and heavier than rock—they are the loyalty and righteousness inscribed in the bones of the Chinese people, the torch of spirit passed down from generation to generation in Shanxi, never extinguished.
